notable_claims: The president of East Stroudsburg University removed newsgroups deemed offensive.
classification.summary: A report indicates that the president of East Stroudsburg University, a public institution in Pennsylvania, ordered the removal of several Usenet newsgroups. The censorship was reportedly based on the grounds that the content of these groups was offensive to some individuals.
classification.title: Censorship of some newsgroups at my school - what can I do?

identity.subject: Censorship of some newsgroups at my school - what can I do?

notable_claims: College administrators ordered the removal of specific newsgroups because they were deemed offensive by a third party.
classification.summary: Daniel Garcia reports that his college administration removed several Usenet newsgroups, specifically erotica binaries, following a complaint from another college president. While the author is not interested in the specific content removed, he expresses concern over the precedent of removing groups based on subjective offensiveness. He seeks historical precedents where schools were forced to restore censored newsgroups.
classification.title: Censorship of some newsgroups at my school - what can I do?

identity.subject: Censorship of some newsgroups at my school - what can I do?

notable_claims: The University of Vienna Computer Center banned groups including alt.binaries.pictures.erotica and alt.sex.bestiality.
classification.summary: A repost reporting that several Usenet newsgroups, primarily focused on erotica and tasteless content, were banned at the University of Vienna Computer Center. The original report was written in German.
classification.title: Info ueber gesperrte Gruppen an der UNI-Wien

identity.subject: [at.kultur, et al.]  Info ueber gesperrte Gruppen an der UNI-Wien

notable_claims: The Academic Senate unanimously decided to prevent university members from accessing pornographic image material.
Specific newsgroups including alt.binaries.pictures.erotica and alt.sex.pictures were targeted for deletion.
The University of Vienna explicitly stated it would not act as a censorship authority for other institutions.
classification.summary: Gerhard Winkler reports on a decision by the Academic Senate of the University of Vienna to block access to pornographic image material and Neo-Nazi content on university networks. The senate specifically ordered the deletion and blocking of several 'alt.binaries' and 'alt.sex' newsgroups. The administration noted that while they are restricting their own server, they do not view themselves as a censorship authority for other universities.
classification.title: Info ueber gesperrte Gruppen an der UNI-Wien

identity.subject: Info ueber gesperrte Gruppen an der UNI-Wien

notable_claims: Daniel J. Karnes threatened legal action over content in the net.legends FAQ.
classification.summary: The editor of the net.legends FAQ, based at the University of Tennessee Knoxville, reports receiving threats of legal action from Daniel J. Karnes. The dispute concerns content written about Karnes within the FAQ file. The author characterizes these legal threats as baseless.
classification.title: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

identity.subject: [comp.org.eff.talk]  Re: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

classification.summary: A cross-posted newsgroup message regarding threats involving Daniel J. Karnes. The post appears in multiple forums including comp.org.eff.talk and news.admin.policy, indicating a dispute crossing technical administration and legal/civil liberties boundaries.
classification.title: Re: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

identity.subject: Re: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

notable_claims: The FAQ aimed to provide profiles of individuals based on their public Usenet posting habits and style.
classification.summary: David DeLaney responds to legal threats made by Daniel J. Karnes regarding an FAQ that profiled 'famous or infamous' individuals on Usenet. DeLaney defends the purpose of the FAQ as providing context for users and notes that the profiles are based on public posting habits. The exchange highlights early tensions between online community profiling, personal reputation, and legal threats in the Usenet era.
classification.title: Re: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

identity.subject: Re: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

notable_claims: Written statements are categorized as libel rather than slander.
The author claims that Usenet profiles based on public postings are factual representations of a user's 'face shown to the world'.
classification.summary: David DeLaney responds to legal threats of slander and libel made by Daniel J. Karnes regarding a profile or FAQ entry written about Karnes's Usenet activity. DeLaney defends the factual nature of his descriptions, including discussions of aliases like 'Artimus Page'. The exchange highlights early internet conflicts over online identity, reputation management, and the application of defamation law to Usenet postings.
classification.title: 02/Re: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

notable_claims: The author claims that the UTCC administration is disjoint from other university computer systems like enigma.phys.utk.edu.
The author asserts that Karnes is one of the most well-known names on Usenet and therefore belongs on a list of prominent users.
classification.summary: David Delaney responds to threats made by Daniel J. Karnes regarding the inclusion of Karnes' name in a Usenet FAQ list of well-known users. The exchange involves disputes over censorship, harassment of university computing centers (UTCC), and the distinction between different administrative entities at the University of Tennessee. It highlights early conflicts over online reputation, public lists of 'kooks' or famous users, and the boundaries of acceptable UseNet behavior.
classification.title: 03/Re: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

notable_claims: Public schools funded by state legislatures may be legally prohibited from censoring employee email or speech due to constitutional guarantees.
classification.summary: David Delaney responds to legal threats from Daniel J. Karnes regarding email communications at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville (UTK). Delaney argues that as a public institution, UTK cannot legally censor employee speech or email without violating constitutional free speech guarantees. He crossposts the discussion to EFF-related groups to seek expert opinions on academic freedom and censorship.
classification.title: 04/Re: Threats from Daniel J. Karnes

notable_claims: The Swinburne U. of Technology computer policy contains excellent provisions for freedom of expression, due process, and privacy.
classification.summary: A reposted critique and analysis of the computer usage policy at Swinburne University of Technology in Australia. The author characterizes the policy as a positive example of institutional governance.
classification.title: Swinburne U. of Technology (Australia) computer policy

identity.subject: Re: Swinburne U. of Technology (Australia) computer policy

notable_claims: The Swinburne policy explicitly states that rules governing academic freedom apply to the use of communications networks for the pursuit of knowledge.
The policy prohibits university employees from intercepting private electronic data without written consent from the Vice-Chancellor or the addressee.
Access to computer networks may only be refused after due process.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the Network Access and Code of Practice Policy of Swinburne University of Technology. He praises the policy for explicitly applying academic freedom rules to communications networks and providing strong privacy protections against unauthorized interception by employees. The post highlights a model for due process and freedom of expression in university computer policies.
classification.title: Re: Swinburne U. of Technology (Australia) computer policy

identity.subject: Re: Swinburne U. of Technology (Australia) computer policy

notable_claims: UMass AUP privacy protections are described as too vague to be effective.
The UMass AUP requires labeling of offensive material despite explicitly rejecting censorship.
classification.summary: This item is a reposted critique of the University of Massachusetts University Computing Services Acceptable Use Policy (AUP). The critique argues that the policy's privacy protections are too vague and that due process is ignored for certain offenses. It further notes a contradiction where censorship is rejected, yet the labeling of 'offensive' material is mandated.
classification.title: AUP Review - UMass

notable_claims: The UMass policy allows unannounced inspection of client files, jobs, and terminal sessions.
Requiring the labeling of 'objectionable' material is viewed as a censor's tool according to ALA interpretations of the Library Bill of Rights.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the University of Massachusetts Computer Use Policy, specifically questioning the lack of due process and the authority behind unannounced file inspections. He argues that requiring users to label 'objectionable' material is a form of censorship contrary to intellectual freedom. To support his argument, he references American Library Association guidelines against labeling books.
classification.title: Re: [comp.admin.policy] AUP Review - UMass

notable_claims: The Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it.
Censoring computer networks is futile compared to existing uncensored communication like telephones and mail.
classification.summary: A forwarded paraphrase of an article by Howard Rheingold in the San Francisco Examiner. The piece argues against cyberspace censorship, suggesting that network architecture naturally bypasses restrictions and that education is a better solution than prohibition.
classification.title: [SF Examiner] "Why Censoring Cyberspace Is Futile"

notable_claims: The Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it.
The Internet's decentralized design, originally intended to withstand nuclear attack, makes centralized control impossible.
classification.summary: Howard Rheingold argues that government censorship of the Internet is technically impossible due to its decentralized architecture. He suggests that instead of legislative restrictions, society should focus on educating children and cultivating personal moral grounding to navigate an uncensorable digital environment.
classification.title: Why Censoring Cyberspace Is Futile
